title: Job 15:17–35
context: Eliphaz, still speaking, appeals to the tradition of the fathers and describes at length the anxious life and certain ruin of the wicked man who defies God. The portrait draws on a common view that the wicked always suffer in this life; Job will challenge that view directly (21:7). Eliphaz does not name Job, but the description, with its fire and lost branches, seems aimed at him. The notes report his speech without treating it as the book’s doctrine.

verses.text: “I will show you, listen to me; that which I have seen I will declare
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says, I will show you, listen to me; that which I have seen I will declare. Arminian readers see a man confident in his own observation, unaware of its limits.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Eliphaz grounds his teaching in personal experience. In chapter 4 he appealed to a night vision; here he appeals to what he has seen.

verses.text: (which wise men have told by their fathers, and have not hidden it;
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz appeals to what wise men have received from their fathers. Arminian readers see tradition offered as authority, which can preserve wisdom but can also preserve error.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the friends rely heavily on inherited wisdom. The book honors tradition but shows that it cannot answer every question about suffering.

verses.text: to whom alone the land was given, and no stranger passed among them):
verses.arminianNotes: These fathers received the land alone, with no stranger among them. Arminian readers note that Eliphaz claims a pure, unmixed tradition, though the exact reference is uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the verse is difficult and that its meaning is debated. Eliphaz seems to claim that his tradition is untainted by outside influence.

verses.text: the wicked man writhes in pain all his days, even the number of years that are laid up for the oppressor.
verses.arminianNotes: The wicked man writhes in pain all his days. Arminian readers see Eliphaz stating the traditional view that the wicked suffer inwardly throughout their lives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Scripture affirms the unrest of the wicked in places (Isaiah 57:20-21), but Job will point out that the wicked often prosper (21:7). Eliphaz’s rule is too rigid.

verses.text: A sound of terrors is in his ears. In prosperity the destroyer will come on him.
verses.arminianNotes: A sound of terrors is in his ears; in prosperity the destroyer comes. Arminian readers see Eliphaz picturing a guilty conscience that can never rest even in good times.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers suspect that this picture of sudden destruction in prosperity seems to echo Job’s own story. Eliphaz may be hinting that Job’s losses reveal his wickedness.

verses.text: He doesn’t believe that he will return out of darkness. He is waited for by the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: He does not believe he will return out of darkness; the sword waits for him. Arminian readers see a picture of hopelessness that Eliphaz assigns to the wicked.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job has expressed hopelessness, and Eliphaz may be turning Job’s own words against him. The friend is drawing a portrait meant to fit Job.

verses.text: He wanders abroad for bread, saying, ‘Where is it?’ He knows that the day of darkness is ready at his hand.
verses.arminianNotes: He wanders for bread, asking where it is, knowing the day of darkness is near. Arminian readers see the insecurity Eliphaz attributes to the wicked, who can never be sure of their next meal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the image of wandering for food suggests utter loss. Eliphaz describes the wicked as reduced to beggary as their judgment approaches.

verses.text: Distress and anguish make him afraid. They prevail against him, as a king ready to the battle.
verses.arminianNotes: Distress and anguish overwhelm him like a king ready for battle. Arminian readers see the vivid image of fear attacking the wicked man as an army attacks a city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the military image stresses inescapable dread. Eliphaz paints the wicked as besieged by their own fears, with no way of escape from the dread that surrounds them.

verses.text: Because he has stretched out his hand against God, and behaves himself proudly against the Almighty,
verses.arminianNotes: The wicked man has stretched out his hand against God and behaves himself proudly against the Almighty. Arminian readers see Eliphaz naming defiance of God as the root of the wicked man’s fate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that pride against God is indeed condemned throughout Scripture. Eliphaz’s error lies in implying, without evidence, that Job is such a man.

verses.text: he runs at him with a stiff neck, with the thick shields of his bucklers,
verses.arminianNotes: He runs at God with a stiff neck and thick shields. Arminian readers see open rebellion portrayed, a man charging at God as if in battle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the image of attacking God may be aimed at Job’s bold complaints. Eliphaz interprets Job’s lament as an assault on the Almighty.

verses.text: because he has covered his face with his fatness, and gathered fat on his thighs.
verses.arminianNotes: He has covered his face with fat and gathered fat on his thighs. Arminian readers see prosperity and self-indulgence as the setting for the wicked man’s arrogance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that fatness in the Old Testament sometimes symbolizes complacency and insensitivity toward God (Deuteronomy 32:15). Eliphaz links wealth with pride and spiritual dullness.

verses.text: He has lived in desolate cities, in houses which no one inhabited, which were ready to become heaps.
verses.arminianNotes: He has lived in desolate cities and houses ready to become heaps. Arminian readers see the wicked man’s security proving hollow, his dwelling places destined for ruin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the meaning of the verse is debated; it may describe the wicked rebuilding cursed places or simply living amid desolation and decay.

verses.text: He will not be rich, neither will his substance continue, neither will their possessions be extended on the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: He will not be rich, nor will his substance continue. Arminian readers see Eliphaz asserting that ill-gotten wealth never lasts, a common theme in wisdom literature.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Proverbs often affirms the fleeting nature of unjust gain. Eliphaz states the principle as an absolute rule, which Job’s experience challenges.

verses.text: He will not depart out of darkness. The flame will dry up his branches. He will go away by the breath of God’s mouth.
verses.arminianNotes: The flame will dry up his branches, and he will go away by the breath of God’s mouth. Arminian readers note the image of fire, which may recall the fire that consumed Job’s flocks (1:16).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the branches may stand for offspring, which would make the verse painfully pointed toward Job. Eliphaz’s portrait seems drawn to match Job’s losses.

verses.text: Let him not trust in emptiness, deceiving himself, for emptiness will be his reward.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz warns the wicked man not to trust in emptiness, deceiving himself, since emptiness will be his reward. Arminian readers see a warning against false security, a truth that applies widely even if misapplied here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that trusting in emptiness leads to emptiness, a principle found elsewhere in Scripture. Eliphaz’s mistake is assuming that Job trusts in it.

verses.text: It will be accomplished before his time. His branch will not be green.
verses.arminianNotes: It will be accomplished before his time; his branch will not be green. Arminian readers see Eliphaz describing premature death and loss as the fate of the wicked.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the withered branch continues the plant imagery. Eliphaz may be pointing to the loss of Job’s children as evidence of judgment.

verses.text: He will shake off his unripe grape as the vine, and will cast off his flower as the olive tree.
verses.arminianNotes: He will shake off his unripe grape like the vine and cast off his flower like the olive. Arminian readers see fruitlessness, the failure of a life that never comes to maturity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the images of vine and olive losing their fruit stress unfulfilled promise. Eliphaz paints the wicked life as ending before it can bear fruit.

verses.text: For the company of the godless will be barren, and fire will consume the tents of bribery.
verses.arminianNotes: The company of the godless will be barren, and fire will consume the tents of bribery. Arminian readers see Eliphaz linking godlessness with injustice, both doomed to destruction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the reference to bribery suggests corrupt dealing. Perhaps Eliphaz is suggesting that Job’s wealth was gained unjustly, a charge he makes more openly in 22:6-9.

verses.text: They conceive mischief and produce iniquity. Their heart prepares deceit.”
verses.arminianNotes: They conceive mischief and produce iniquity; their heart prepares deceit. Arminian readers see sin’s progression from inner intention to outward act, a pattern Scripture often describes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear echoes of Psalm 7:14 and Isaiah 59:4. As a description of the wicked it rings true, but as an implied verdict on Job it is the friends’ error, which 42:7 later addresses.
